- Ballotpedia title: "California Proposition 43, Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives and Property Tax Initiative Prohibition Amendment (November 2026)".
- Proponents raised $14.86M as of Sept 19; opponents $4.86M. Total contributions per SOS: $16.39M support / $10.44M opposition.
- Poll: 36% support, 46% oppose (Oct 19-25, IGS/LA Times). Likely to fail.
- Notable: California Democratic Party opposes; CA Republican Party supports; League of Women Voters opposes.

Let me dig deeper into:
1. Who funds the Yes campaign (top contributors) — is it real estate developers, business interests, or taxpayer groups?
2. KQED articles on fiscal impact.
3. CalMatters detailed guide.
4. The withdrawn HJTA initiative — what it would have done (retroactive invalidation, transfer tax limits) — context for the compromise.
5. Editorial endorsements list (Sac Bee no, SDUT yes, SF Chronicle yes, Santa Cruz Sentinel no, Press Democrat no, Southern California News Group yes).
6. Also SPUR's recommendation.

Let me also look at the evidence about whether 2/3 requirements are good policy — e.g., research on how Prop 13's 2/3 requirement pushed local governments to fees, assessments, and debt; also the "special interests pass earmarked taxes with fewer votes" claim.

Also consider whether Prop 43's ad valorem prohibition (section b) has significant effects: it would prevent charter cities from imposing real estate transfer taxes via initiative? Hmm, Art XIII A Sec 1(a) already limits ad valorem property taxes to 1% for general taxes; Art XIII D Sec 3(a) prohibits local governments from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property except the 1% cap and bond taxes. Courts have held real estate transfer taxes are "transactions taxes" and Art XIII D prohibits "transactions or rights or privileges" taxes on real property for local governments (Bldg. Industry Assn. v. City of San Jose?). Actually, Art XIII D Sec 3(a) says "No local government may impose ad valorem taxes on real property, or transactions or rights or privileges on property, except as follows: ..." — so charter cities' transfer taxes were arguably prohibited, but the courts in 2010 (Bldg. Indus. Assn of Central Coast v. County of Santa Barbara?) Hmm. There's a 2025 case about Measure ULA: LA Superior Court Judge ruled ULA invalid in 2024? Let me check: In August 2024, an LA Superior Court judge ruled... Actually I recall a judge upheld ULA in 2024, and the Court of Appeal in 2025 affirmed? Let me search.

Anyway. Let's dig into the important questions for making a recommendation:
- Effect on local service funding (real examples).
- Effect on who benefits (corporate interests vs. taxpayers).
- Democratic principle: supermajority requirements for tax increases.

Let me fetch KQED articles, CalMatters guide, SPUR guide, and campaign finance details.

Why Opponents of Prop. 43 Say It Would Cripple Local Funding
Opponents of Proposition 43 warn that requiring a two-thirds vote for citizen-led special taxes would choke off local revenue as federal funding dries up.
Oct 6, 2026
Updated 5:32 pm PT
Scott Shafer (https://www.kqed.org/author/scottshafer) Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
Listen
LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA- MAY 5: In this photo illustration, an official voter information guide mailed to a Southern California resident, ahead of a state primary election, photographed May 5, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo Illustration by Jay L Clendenin/Getty Images)
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would raise the requirement for increasing special taxes placed on the ballot by citizens. Right now it takes a simple majority to pass those taxes, but Prop. 43 would require a two-thirds vote.
The initiative is supported by business groups and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. Meanwhile, unions and the California League of Cities say Prop. 43 would cripple their ability to raise critical revenue at a time when the federal government is slashing funding to state and local governments.
Scott and Marisa talk to the No on 43 campaign’s Bill Barnes, who is director of campaigns and community engagement for the Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California. Marisa previously discussed the Yes campaign with Jon Coupal (https://www.kqed.org/news/12095893/prop-43-would-make-it-harder-to-raise-local-taxes-can-it-pass), president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.
Don’t forget to use KQED’s voter guide (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide) when filling out your ballot!
Plus, check out Political Breakdown’s weekly newsletter (https://www.kqed.org/newsletters/political-breakdown), delivered straight to your inbox.

Prop. 43 Would Make It Harder to Raise Local Taxes. Can It Pass?
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, an anti-tax group who brought California the landmark Proposition 13, is now sponsoring Proposition 43 — a measure to make it harder for cities and counties to raise local taxes.
Aug 18, 2026
Updated Oct 6, 2026
Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
Listen
Close-up of ballot drop box outside of polling place
This November, California voters will consider Proposition 43 — a measure aimed at making it harder for cities and counties to raise local taxes. It’s sponsored by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. That’s the anti-tax group that brought California Proposition 13 in 1978, a landmark ballot measure limiting property tax increases.
Marisa sits down with the President of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Jon Coupal. They discuss Prop. 43 and California’s broader tax system.
You can also listen to the Non-Profit Housing Association’s Bill Barnes explain the opposition (https://www.kqed.org/news/12103136/why-opponents-of-prop-43-say-it-would-cripple-local-funding) to Prop. 43.
Check out Political Breakdown’s weekly newsletter (https://www.kqed.org/newsletters/political-breakdown), delivered straight to your inbox.

Proposition 43
Raise vote threshold for special tax measures
This would make it harder to impose or increase local taxes by raising the threshold for local citizen-driven special tax ballot initiatives to pass from a simple majority to two-thirds. The two-thirds threshold already applies to taxes proposed by local governments but not by individuals. The measure reflects a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Prop
43
CA
Prop
43
|
Constitutional Amendment
Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services
Requires two-thirds voter approval to impose, extend, or increase special taxes, specifically eliminating the ability for a citizen initiative to qualify with a simple majority vote.
SPUR's Recommendation
SPUR has consistently called for reforming Prop. 13 and opposed onerous new restrictions on the government’s ability to raise needed revenue. Prop. 43 would take the state in the opposite direction. The measure would cement and expand Prop. 13's legacy by amending the California Constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for imposing or extending any special tax. It would undermine both the democratic principle of majority rule and one of the few remaining pathways for funding important services.
Vote NO
What Prop. 43 Would Do
Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote of the electorate to approve all special taxes, whether placed on the ballot through citizen initiative (voter signatures) or by government officials.
Proposition 13 in 1978 amended the California constitution to limit local governments’ ability to impose, extend, or increase special taxes (taxes dedicated to a specific purpose) by requiring a minimum two-thirds approval by voters. In 2017, the California Supreme Court ruled that taxes placed on the ballot by voters through signature gathering were not subject to this same two-thirds requirement. Prop. 43 seeks to overturn the 2017 decision and amend the constitution to establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval requirement for any new, extended, or increased local special tax, regardless of whether the initiative was placed on the ballot by local government officials or through a voter initiative.
The Backstory
Prop. 43 is the latest proposal in a decades-long series of amendments to the California Constitution that have significantly limited local governments' ability to fund projects and services by imposing new taxes. In 1978, Prop. 13 capped property tax rates at 1% of assessed value and established the initial two-thirds voter requirement to approve special taxes. In 2017, however, the California Supreme Court clarified in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (Upland) that many of the key provisions in the California Constitution restricting the imposition of new taxes applied only to proposals put forward by the government. Consequently, the Upland decision established that new special tax measures submitted through citizen initiative required only a 50% plus one vote majority to pass rather than two-thirds approval. 1 Since that decision, a number of local special taxes in California have passed with a simple majority after being placed on the ballot through voter initiative. Such measures account for only a small minority of revenue measures statewide.
Prop. 43 would establish a uniform two-thirds voter-approval threshold for new special taxes regardless of how they were placed on the ballot. The California Legislature placed the proposition on the ballot after reaching a compromise with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, which had another, similar proposal to amend the California Constitution. 2 That proposal had qualified for the November 2026 ballot through a voter signature-gathering campaign. The compromise sidelines some of the more complex issues in the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association’s proposed amendment and instead offers a simplified amendment focused only on the voter threshold.
Prop. 43 requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Prop. 43 would make it significantly more difficult to raise revenues for local government services and projects by requiring a higher approval threshold. It is likely that the resulting fiscal impacts to government, in the form of unfunded programs or expiring taxes that can no longer be renewed, would fall most heavily on lower-income residents and people of color. In the Bay Area, for example, the citizen initiative process has recently been used to propose taxes to support transit operations and has been discussed as a potential future pathway to place a regional affordable housing bond before the voters. Transit operations and affordable housing are both examples of government expenditures that disproportionately benefit lower-income residents and people of color and that will be difficult to sustain without viable approaches to securing new revenues.
Additionally, placing broad restrictions on how the electorate can raise taxes can drive the government to seek other, less equitable sources of revenue. The severe limitations Prop. 13 placed on property taxes, for example, have, among other factors, helped drive local governments to increasingly rely on sales taxes, a much more regressive revenue source.
Pros
Prop. 43 would simplify existing law and establish a consistent, uniform voter threshold for imposing, extending, or increasing new special taxes.
The measure would maintain the 50% plus one vote threshold for passing general taxes (those not dedicated to a specific purpose).
Cons
Prop. 43 would undermine the basic principle of majority rule by imposing a heightened approval threshold on certain voter-proposed initiatives.
The measure would continue and expand on the legacy of Prop. 13, a law that has profoundly distorted California’s tax structure, fueled wealth inequality, and exacerbated the state’s housing challenges by disincentivizing home sales and turnover.
It would eliminate one of the few viable ways to raise local revenues at a time when local governments' fiscal needs are especially acute.

Guest Commentary written by Susan Shelley Susan Shelley is the vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The November ballot measure Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/) would make it harder to raise taxes in California by restoring the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. A “special tax” is one that earmarks the revenue for specific purposes. Ever since voters approved Proposition 13 in 1978 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)), the California Constitution has clearly stated that cities, counties and special districts may impose special taxes “by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district.” If courts had enforced that plain language, Californians today would not be paying billions of dollars in local taxes. This includes sales tax increases such as L.A. County’s 2024 Measure A (https://homeless.lacounty.gov/measure-a/) for homelessness programs, as well as Measure ULA in the city of Los Angeles (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/), a real estate transfer tax on the value of a property worth more than $5 million, which also pays for homelessness programs and affordable housing. Neither of these received the constitutionally required 66.67% of the vote. In San Francisco, courts upheld a June 2018 special tax (http://sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-appeals-court-upholds-S-F-s-commercial-15903302.php) on commercial real estate leases to fund early education and child care, and a November 2018 special tax on the gross receipts of businesses to pay for homelessness programs. Just like Los Angeles, these measures fell short of a two-thirds vote. In 1978, the people of California added the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes to their constitution. When did the constitution become merely advisory? READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Minority rule in California? How Proposition 43 would tie the hands of local governments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/) It began in 2017 with ambiguous language in a California Supreme Court decision, California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland (https://cases.justia.com/california/supreme-court/2017-s234148.pdf?ts=1503939675) . The court suggested — without really deciding — that if a tax increase was placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative instead of by a city council or other government body, the constitution didn’t necessarily apply, and a two-thirds vote wasn’t necessarily required. Lower courts used that language to uphold special taxes that received less than a two-thirds vote if they were placed on the ballot by voters signing initiative petitions. But who are these citizens who want to stand outside grocery stores and farmer’s markets with clipboards to raise their own taxes? They’re often the people who will get the money from the tax. The Upland decision has essentially enabled special interest groups (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) to write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves, pay to collect the signatures to get it on the ballot, and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Some of the court rulings on these Upland taxes have even allowed local government officials to work hand-in-glove with special interests (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/the-fiction-of-citizens-tax-initiatives-in-california/) to get tax increases on the ballot as “citizens’ initiatives.” Now the state government is pushing the envelope even further. The governor recently signed Assembly Bill 1923 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1923), requiring the Fresno County Registrar of Voters to place a citizens’ initiative sales tax increase for transportation on the November ballot (https://fresnoland.org/2026/08/06/better-roads/). The state did this over the objections of the Fresno County Board of Supervisors after it lawfully exercised its discretion under the elections code to order a study of the measure, which would have delayed it past the 2026 ballot deadline and placed it on the 2028 ballot. This is no way to run a railroad. There is no “citizens’ initiative tax increase exception” from the two-thirds vote requirement in Prop. 13. Courts have simply made it up. Californians who are already struggling with the high cost of living have been forced to pay even higher prices because judges have made it easier to raise taxes. Prop. 43 will restore the two-thirds vote requirement for all local special taxes, including any tax increases placed on the ballot by a citizens’ initiative. It’s a constitutional amendment, overriding court precedents that say otherwise. General taxes, such as those that direct the revenue into a city or county general fund to be spent as elected officials decide, would continue to require only a simple majority vote. Some local government officials may believe voters will not approve general taxes, so they would prefer to tell voters the money from a new tax will be spent only on a specific, urgent need. Their problem isn’t the constitution, it’s trust — if voters don’t trust local elected officials to spend tax money on the most important priorities first, a majority may vote ‘no’ on any tax unless they know what it will fund and it’s guaranteed in writing. Those same officials undoubtedly benefit from having a court-created loophole to raise special taxes without the need for a two-thirds vote. The loophole has been growing with every election. Multiple “citizens’ initiative” tax increases are on the November ballot, racing to squeeze through the opening before voters can hammer boards over it. Prop. 43 gives California voters the opportunity to restore what state courts have eroded: a taxpayer protection in the state constitution that requires local special taxes to have the approval of two-thirds of voters to pass. Guest Commentary written by Sandra Lowe Sandra Lowe is a member of the Sonoma City Council and a longtime political consultant. Sometimes things that sound simple are not. Buried in the list of ballot questions this November that could shape our tax code and California’s progress is an effort to strike a blow to the most fundamental democratic principle which guides our local governments’ decisions: majority rule. Local government is elected by majority, pass policy by majority, approve construction projects by majority and, yes, pass taxes by majority. Prop. 43 raises the threshold for local tax measures from a simple majority to two-thirds, allowing the minority to win. It must be rejected. In Sonoma County, one of the highest fire-risk areas in California, citizens passed Measure H (https://sonomacounty.gov/administrative-support-and-fiscal-services/county-executives-office/strategic-initiatives/fire-services-project/measure-h) in 2024. Measure H raises revenue through a half-cent sales tax to support emergency services. The dedicated funding ensures sustainable fire response, expanded paramedic availability and aggressive wildfire prevention. In addition to my role as a Sonoma city councilwoman, I serve on the Measure H oversight committee. Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote (https://ballotpedia.org/Sonoma_County,_California,_Measure_H,_Fire_Prevention_and_Disaster_Response_Sales_Tax_Measure_(March_2024)). Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders. No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent. Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions. The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding (https://health.alamedacountyca.gov/program/measures-a-c-and-w/) and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation (https://www.openspaceauthority.org/whats-new/press-release-measure-d). Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime. Last year we were able to expand 24/7 emergency medical response teams, implement vegetation management, provide emergency response during flooding, update fire engines, provide more protective gear, install new technologies to improve firefighting capabilities and initiate community education programs. 

If Prop. 43 was law two years ago, none of that would have happened — even with almost 62% of the vote.

The largest portion of local budgets is public safety. Fire, sheriff and police services are the basics. We don’t have to look too far in our recent history to find catastrophic events which demanded the expert heroic services of our first responders.

No one wants to see response times increase. No one wants to surplus an ambulance or a fire engine. Sonoma County, Altadena, Pacific Palisades — these are not rarities in a world where climate disasters are frequent.

Local governments must not lose the ability to fund vital functions.

The broad range of services Californians are accustomed to receiving could be slashed. Prop. 43’s unfair threshold would have doomed measures such as Alameda County’s 2025 measure for healthcare funding and Santa Clara’s June measure for open space preservation.  

Citizens have high expectations for local government. They expect us to deliver a wide range of services. Prop. 43 would tie the hands of local governments statewide, allowing a slim minority to determine the outcomes of ballot issues and disenfranchise voters. Prop. 43 would take us backward and begin round after round of service cuts, potentially making California less protected from disasters and more vulnerable to crime.

Majority rule is the basis of our democracy and a hallmark of a free society. Let's not go backward.

Confused about how to vote on Proposition 43? Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 7:54 AM
Proposition 43 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article316990490.html) is billed as a taxpayer protection measure that would “save” Proposition 13.
In reality, it would make it much harder for citizen groups in California to pass tax increases to help pay for critical services such as fire and police protection, flood control, health care facilities and road maintenance. It would also make it harder to fund libraries, parks and affordable housing programs that local governments simply can’t afford.
Prop. 43 seeks to raise the threshold necessary to pass citizen tax initiatives from a simple majority to a supermajority of 66.7%, which would mean 33.3% of voters would be calling the shots.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 43 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article316990490.html)
This is why the combined editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee (https://www.modbee.com/), Merced Sun-Star, (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/) Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) oppose Prop. 43. We strongly urge a “no” vote.
Prop. 43 would give the minority too much power. It would make it much harder for citizens to take matters into their own hands when governments can’t — or won’t — finance special projects that serve the public interest.
The ability to pass special taxes is especially important now, when wildfires, droughts and extreme weather leave so many communities vulnerable. Rather than waiting for disaster to strike — or depending on Washington or Sacramento for financial help that may never come — local tax measures can provide revenue to prepare for emergencies, whether it means hiring more firefighters, upgrading equipment or clearing flood channels.
What supporters say
Anti-tax groups, such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (https://www.hjta.org/saveprop13_about_initiative/) andReform California (https://www.reformcalifornia.org/campaigns/stop-the-tax-hikes), say Prop. 43 would merely close a legal loophole used too often by special-interest groups to fund pet projects on the backs of taxpayers.
They say that Proposition 13, which was passed by voters in 1978, specifies that cities, counties and special districts can impose taxes earmarked for specific purposes only with the approval of a supermajority of voters.
Yet language in Prop. 13 and in a follow-up measure, Prop. 218, is somewhat ambiguous. It does not specify that citizen tax initiatives require a supermajority to pass. In a series of court rulings, judges found that they do not.
We weren’t convinced by Prop. 43’s backers, and voters should be skeptical, too. Nor should they buy into the notion that plenty of money is available if public officials would only stop wasting it on misplaced priorities.
“We can go through any budget, and I will find the cost savings to eliminate the need for a tax increase on any ballot in the state of California this cycle,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, the head of Reform California, told us.
Never mind that federal and state budget cuts have taken a huge financial toll on local government. Sacramento County, for example, faced a $101 million budget shortfall this year. Atleast half the deficit (https://cue.gcp.misitemgr.com/cue-web/#/main?uri=https://cue.gcp.misitemgr.com/webservice/escenic/container/ac765bdc-7f13-11f1-a011-277da135f0d0&mimetype=x-ece/container&extra=%7B%22package%22:%22ece-auto-gen-845e918b-ec6d-4d33-a61b-298f753a3360%22%7D) was attributed to cuts in the federal budget.
Communities rely on special taxes for basic services
Local governments have made foolish and, in some cases, corrupt spending decisions, and they should be held accountable.
But Prop. 43 ignores the fact that many communities have no other way to finance needed services.
Take the tiny community of Crockett, population 3,000, located in Contra Costa County.
Volunteers with the Crockett Improvement Association assumed responsibility for landscaping and maintenance of public spaces — a job that included picking up litter, trimming bushes and maintaining streetlights. But when the work became too onerous for aging volunteers, the group gathered signatures to put a $50-a-year parcel tax (https://ballotpedia.org/Crockett_Community_Services_District,_California,_Measure_L,_Maintenance_and_Landscaping_Tax_Initiative_(November_2022)) on the ballot. It passed by 62.78%.
That’s impressive support, yet under Prop. 43, the measure would have failed. Then what? Allow trash and weeds and overgrown bushes to encroach on public spaces?
From a practical standpoint, special taxes are the only way some specific needs can be met, and requiring supermajority approval can create hardships — and even dangers — for communities large and small.
A more reasonable threshold — say 55%, which is the margin required to pass school facility bonds — would be a fair compromise to consider in the future.
For now, voters must decide whether to allow a small minority of voters to dictate whether tax measures should pass. We don’t believe they should.

# California transit, transportation leaders announce opposition to Prop 43
Prop 43 would require a two-thirds supermajority for special taxes that voters place on the ballot through citizen initiative.
Today, those measures pass with a simple majority.
This November, Bay Area voters are deciding on two major transit measures that reached the ballot exactly this way: San Francisco’s Prop H for Muni and the five-county Regional Measure RTM for BART, Muni, Caltrain and AC Transit.
Under Prop 43’s rules, measures like these would need two-thirds of the vote to pass.
...
San Francisco Prop H would fund Muni operations with a parcel tax for 15 years, raising an estimated $160 million or more a year to help close SFMTA’s operating deficit.
It qualified after San Franciscans signed a citizen petition, so it needs a simple majority to pass.
Regional Measure RTM would fund BART, Muni, Caltrain and AC Transit with a sales tax across Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties.
It would raise roughly $1 billion a year for 14 years.
More than 235,000 valid voter signatures put it on the ballot, and it needs a simple majority to pass.
Under Prop 43, a measure like Prop H or RTM would need two-thirds of the vote.
A measure supported by 60 percent or more of voters could still fail.

The government-placed path already requires 2/3, and a huge number of local special taxes pass with 2/3 (e.g., most school parcel taxes, most transportation sales taxes which require 2/3 by statute). So the measure doesn't eliminate the ability to fund services via special taxes — it just means they need 2/3 support (as has been the case for the vast majority of local special taxes since 1978). The citizen-initiative majority path is a relatively recent development (2017 onward) and accounts for "only a small minority of revenue measures statewide" (per SPUR).

Arguments for NO:
1. Undermines the initiative right — the people's power to legislate — and majority rule; supermajority requirements give 33.4% veto power. Research on supermajority tax requirements suggests they distort policy: they push governments to less transparent revenue tools (fees, assessments, debt), reduce local fiscal capacity, and can lead to worse budgeting.
2. Real-world harms: measures like Sonoma County Measure H (fire, 62%), Alameda County Measure B (healthcare), Santa Clara Measure D (open space), LA Measure ULA (affordable housing/homelessness), SF Prop C (homelessness), Crockett parcel tax (62.8%) would have failed. These fund fire protection, health care, housing, transit, parks.
3. Timing/context: federal cuts to state and local funding, wildfire risk, transit fiscal cliffs — local revenue need is acute.
4. Who funds it: California Business Roundtable (70%), commercial landlords — the entities most likely to pay these taxes. This suggests the measure's purpose is to protect a specific set of payers rather than taxpayers generally.
5. It could distort revenue toward more regressive sources (sales taxes, fees) — SPUR notes Prop 13's limits drove reliance on sales taxes.
6. The measure's ad valorem provision (section (b)) is vague and could have unforeseen consequences (e.g., blocking local property-value-based taxes, possibly affecting things like local real estate transfer taxes used for homelessness).
7. The measure was written by an Assemblymember who opposes it; passed nearly unanimously as a legislative compromise, not because of substantive consensus — arguably a deal cut under pressure to remove HJTA's more extreme initiative (which would have retroactively killed existing taxes and capped transfer taxes). That deal was itself the "win" for local governments. But a "No" vote doesn't bring back the HJTA initiative; that was already withdrawn. So the compromise is done. Voting No now just leaves the status quo (majority vote for citizen special taxes).

Hmm, an important consideration: If Prop 43 fails, does HJTA come back with the more sweeping initiative in 2028? Possibly, but they'd need to re-qualify; and the 2024 Supreme Court ruling (Legislature v. Weber) said the more far-reaching Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act was an unconstitutional revision via initiative. That means the more sweeping measure can only be enacted by legislative referral — which the Legislature just did in narrower form. So a "No" vote on 43 doesn't automatically bring back the extreme version; it would require legislative cooperation (2/3), which happened only because of deal pressure. Hmm, but the Legislature did agree to the compromise, meaning they'd potentially be pressured again.

Now, normative judgment. Which is "better"? Let's think about the underlying policy question: should citizen-initiated local special taxes require 2/3?

Considerations about democratic legitimacy: The initiative power in California is reserved to the people (Art. II, Sec. 8), and historically courts hold that ambiguities in the initiative power are resolved in favor of the people. Applying supermajority requirements to the people's own exercise of power raises the bar on a fundamental right. Also, there's a substantive asymmetry: when a city council proposes a special tax, it's government acting; when citizens propose, it's the electorate acting. Many scholars argue that the 2/3 requirement should apply uniformly (as Prop 13's text suggests: "by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district" — Art XIII A Sec 4 actually says special taxes by "the city, county and special district" require 2/3 — the text says "Cities, Counties and special districts may impose special taxes ... by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district" — so it limits the government entities, not the electorate; that's the basis of the Upland decision. And Art XIII C Sec 2(d) says "No local government may impose, extend, or increase any special tax unless..." — "local government" is defined in Art XIII C Sec 1 as "any county, city, city and county, including a charter city or county, any special district, or any other local or regional governmental entity." So the courts read it as not including the electorate exercising initiative power. Hmm, but actually Art XIII C Sec 1(a) definition of "local government" — and in Cannabis Coalition v. Upland, the court said the electorate acting through initiative is not "local government" for purposes of the timing restriction. Lower courts extended this to the 2/3 requirement for special taxes.

So legally, the "loophole" framing is defensible: the text limits governments, and courts extended that to exclude the electorate. Supporters say voters who passed Prop 13 and 218 intended all special taxes to require 2/3. Opponents say the initiative is a separate power reserved to the people and that Prop 13's own text says what it says.

1. Empirical: How often do citizen-initiated special taxes pass between 50% and 66.7%? CalMatters reported "over two dozen" such measures since 2017. That's a small number relative to thousands of local measures. So the direct fiscal effect is modest, but symbolically significant.

Measure A passed with 57.7% in March 2024; it was placed by the LA County Board? Actually HJTA claims it was a citizen initiative? Let me verify. LA County Measure A (2024) was the homeless services sales tax replacing Measure H — I believe it was placed on the ballot by the Board of Supervisors... but then it would have needed 2/3 and it passed with 57%. Hmm. Let me check: Measure A passed with 57.7%, which is less than 2/3 — so it must have been qualified as an initiative. Indeed, HJTA/advocates structured it as an initiative. Actually I recall LA County Measure A (March 2024) was placed via citizen initiative by United to House LA / labor coalition. Let me verify.

Alameda County Measure B (2025, healthcare) — passed with ~?

Crockett CSD Measure L (2022, $50 parcel tax, 62.78%).

So many of these are progressive/service-oriented taxes funded by citizens' groups when local boards wouldn't place them (or to avoid the 2/3 hurdle).

Special taxes passed via initiative tend to be: business taxes (SF Prop C, gross receipts; LA ULA on commercial/high-value property), sales taxes (regressive), parcel taxes (per-parcel, regressive), utility users taxes. Special taxes are earmarked and hard to change; requiring broad consensus for permanent, purpose-dedicated taxes (e.g., LA Measure A is a half-cent sales tax in perpetuity with no sunset, approved by 55.7%) is defensible. Permanent, no-sunset tax increases with slim margins is a legitimate concern.
3. Voters have repeatedly endorsed supermajority requirements for special taxes: Prop 13 (1978), Prop 62 (1986), Prop 218 (1996); PPIC found 58% oppose allowing local special taxes to pass by simple majority instead of 2/3 (in the older study) and ~48% of likely voters said the 2/3 requirement had a good effect on services. So there's durable public support for the 2/3 principle.
4. Two-thirds is achievable: most local special taxes pass 2/3 anyway (2024 primary: 75.8% passage rate). It just requires broad consensus and better-designed measures.
5. Prospective only, no retroactive invalidation; narrower than HJTA's initiative.

Hmm. This is a genuinely close call. Let me think about which side has stronger policy evidence.

The core issue: Is the majority-vote path for citizen-initiated special taxes a net benefit or net harm for Californians?

Evidence on the fiscal consequences: The 2/3 requirement (as applied to government-placed special taxes since 1978) has not prevented local revenue growth in aggregate (PPIC: "not much distinctive about California's revenue and spending patterns"; total state/local spending has increased via fees, bonds, sales taxes). It has, however, distorted the revenue mix toward less transparent and often more regressive sources (fees, sales taxes, assessments), and it has caused "fiscalization of land use" that harms housing supply. Adding the citizen-initiative path to the 2/3 rule would extend these distortions modestly.

Evidence on the specific measures blocked: LA Measure A ($1.1B/yr for homelessness, permanent, no sunset, 55.7%); SF Prop C (homelessness, business gross receipts tax, 61%); LA Measure ULA ($830M-$1.4B raised for affordable housing/homelessness, 57.8%); Sonoma Measure H (fire/emergency services, 62%); Alameda County Measure B (healthcare); Santa Clara Measure D (open space); San Diego Measure C (hotel tax, 65%); Crockett parcel tax (62.8%). Under Prop 43, none of these would have passed — that's roughly $2B+ annually in LA alone.

But is the loss of those revenues a net negative? For someone concerned about homelessness services, fire protection, healthcare — yes, clearly negative. For someone concerned about the cost of living, business climate, and taxes on commercial property — positive. Note Measure ULA is widely criticized (it reduced property transactions, hurt small commercial sales, raised costs for affordable housing developers too); LA is considering rolling it back. SF Prop C taxes businesses and is criticized as driving business exodus. LA County Measure A is a permanent half-cent sales tax increase (regressive) for homelessness — the county already had a quarter-cent Measure H; Measure A doubles it with no sunset; and LA County homelessness spending has been criticized for poor results (though LAHSA reformed).

Hmm. So the taxes blocked by Prop 43 are not obviously "good" taxes. Many are regressive sales taxes. Interesting nuance: the pro-43 argument emphasizes cost of living; the anti-43 argument emphasizes service funding.

Consider also the distributional question: Who has the resources to run a 2/3 campaign? Both business groups (No campaign needs money to defeat — actually blocking is cheaper than passing) — under a 2/3 rule, opponents (typically well-funded business interests) have a big structural advantage: they need only 33.4% + 1. Since the Yes side of Prop 43 is funded by business/landlord money, and the taxes blocked tend to be business taxes and sales taxes, the effect is likely to tilt the balance toward blocking business taxes. That's a substantive concern about who wins.

Conversely, under majority rule, well-funded proponents (unions, advocacy groups, or wealthy individuals like Marc Benioff funding SF Prop C) can pass taxes with slim margins — HJTA's point about "special interests write their own tax increase, direct all the money to themselves."

Now, the democratic principle: Should the people's initiative power be subject to a supermajority? The California Supreme Court has repeatedly said the initiative power must be "liberally construed" to protect the people's right. Requiring 2/3 for a voter initiative is unusual — note that statewide initiatives in California need only a majority, even ones that raise state taxes (e.g., Prop 30, Prop 55, Prop 39). So Prop 43 would create an inconsistency: a statewide initiative raising state income taxes needs 50%+1, but a local initiative raising a local special tax needs 2/3. Hmm — though state-level 2/3 legislative requirements exist for legislative tax increases; statewide initiative tax increases need only majority (Prop 13's 2/3 legislative requirement was held in 2012? Actually the courts have held initiatives need only majority — Kennedy Wholesale v. Board of Equalization (1991) held that Prop 13's 2/3 legislative requirement doesn't apply to initiatives, since that would conflict with the initiative power). So the analogy: California's courts have held that supermajority requirements applicable to legislatures don't apply to the people's initiative power (Kennedy Wholesale). Under that logic, applying a 2/3 requirement to citizen initiatives would be inconsistent with how the state-level analogous provision has been treated — and the people would be amending their own constitution to restrict their own initiative power, which is legally permissible but in tension with the historical principle.

Interesting: the 2024 Supreme Court decision (Legislature v. Weber) struck down the 2024 "Taxpayer Protection and Government Accountability Act" as an unconstitutional *revision* — partly because it imposed 2/3 requirements on state taxes too. Now the Legislature itself referred a narrower version.

Given all this, which recommendation?

Let me consider what a thoughtful, nonpartisan policy analysis would say. Notable: the League of Women Voters of California opposes; the California Democratic Party opposes; SEIU, teachers, firefighters oppose; local government associations (League of California Cities, CSAC) oppose. Supporting: HJTA, CA Business Roundtable, CA Taxpayers Association, CA Small Business Association, Reform California, CA Republican Party, family business association, Hispanic chambers of commerce. Editorial boards split: SF Chronicle YES (reluctant), San Diego Union-Tribune YES, Mercury News/East Bay Times YES, Southern California News Group YES; Sacramento Bee/McClatchy NO, Press Democrat NO, Santa Cruz Sentinel NO, LA Times? Let me check the LA Times endorsement. Also PPIC: 51% no / 43% yes.

Let me check the LA Times endorsement and any other major outlets (OC Register YES).

Also let me consider: is there a "harm from failing to pass" scenario? If Prop 43 fails, HJTA may return with more sweeping measures; but as noted, the sweeping retroactive/transfer-tax-cap version is likely an unconstitutional revision via initiative (per Weber) — hmm, actually Weber struck down the 2024 version partly because of its breadth; the 2026 "Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Prop 13" was drafted to be narrower to survive revision challenge. So a No vote leaves open the possibility of a future, more damaging measure (e.g., one capping transfer taxes and retroactively invalidating). Whereas a Yes vote "locks in" the moderate version and HJTA claims victory. But if 43 passes, HJTA might push further (e.g., Prop 41 tax audits, Prop 42 property taxes are on the same ballot).

Conversely, if Prop 43 fails, the status quo remains: majority-vote citizen special taxes, plus continued litigation ambiguity.

Let me weigh expected welfare. I lean toward NO for these reasons:

1. The concrete fiscal harm is documented and substantial: billions in annual revenue for fire/emergency response, healthcare, transit, homelessness, open space, all measures that won majority support (often 55-65%). Blocking them requires no alternative funding source, and the state is already cutting local aid amid federal cuts.

2. The measure restricts the initiative power — the one tool ordinary citizens have when local officials won't act — while doing nothing about government-placed taxes. It converts a majority-rule right into minority veto. The empirical literature on supermajority tax requirements (CBPP, PPIC) shows they don't reduce total spending much but distort the revenue mix toward less transparent, more regressive fees and sales taxes, and they advantage entrenched interests with resources to sustain a blocking 33%.

3. The campaign's funding profile — 70% from the California Business Roundtable, plus commercial landlords — indicates the practical incidence: shielding large commercial property owners/businesses from locally approved taxes (e.g., gross receipts taxes, commercial landlord taxes, transfer taxes). The "taxpayer protection" framing overstates its breadth.

4. The claimed "loophole" is narrow in scope: since 2017, roughly two dozen local measures statewide passed with majority-but-not-2/3 support (out of thousands of local fiscal measures; e.g., 93 in the 2026 local/primary elections alone). So the benefit (consistency, preventing slim-margin earmarked taxes) is modest relative to the cost.

5. There are better solutions than a blanket supermajority: e.g., disclosure of who sponsored "citizen" initiatives, sunset requirements, audit/oversight requirements (Prop 41 addresses audits), or a 55% threshold (as the Sacramento Bee suggests for school bonds). A binary constitutional 2/3 for all local special taxes via initiative is a blunt instrument, especially for small districts (e.g., a 3,000-person community's $50 parcel tax for landscaping) that won 62.8%.

Counterweight: the strongest Yes argument is the gaming problem — officials routing taxes through fake "citizen initiatives" to dodge 2/3 (Alameda County 2018, LA County Measure A 2024, Fresno via AB 1923, Bay Area RTM via SB 63). That's a legitimate democratic concern. But note Prop 43 doesn't distinguish genuine grassroots initiatives from government-orchestrated ones — it raises the bar for all, including genuinely citizen-driven ones in small communities. A targeted fix (e.g., barring government officials/funds from sponsoring "citizen" initiatives, as some proposals would) would address the abuse without restricting the people's power. Also, under Prop 43, the same governments could still route taxes via general taxes (majority) — so the "gaming" incentive partially shifts to less-earmarked general taxes, which arguably is worse for accountability.

I think the balance favors NO. Also the polling: majority of Californians oppose (51-43 PPIC; 46-36 IGS). And the author of the measure opposes it, the League of Women Voters opposes it, and most local-government and public-safety organizations oppose it. Endorsements are split, with several "yes" endorsements grudging ("Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California's tax system").

Hmm, but wait. Let me be careful about being balanced: is there a strong case that the 2/3 rule is actually good? Voters approved 2/3 for special taxes in 1978 and 1996, and PPIC polling shows a majority of Californians support the supermajority for special taxes generally (58% opposed allowing simple majority in the older poll). But the current polling on Prop 43 specifically shows majority opposition — perhaps because the "limits voters' ability" framing.

Let me do a couple more checks: LA Times endorsement, and any analysis of what share of the Yes funding is business vs. taxpayer groups; also check Mercury News/SCNG reasoning and any "No" campaign claims that are overstated (e.g., claim it affects fire/school funding — schools are exempt at 55% via Prop 39 carve-out; fire protection often funded by general taxes or government-placed measures requiring 2/3 anyway).

Important: The No campaign's claim that Prop 43 makes it harder to fund fire/police/schools is partly overstated: (a) school parcel taxes (Prop 39 bonds at 55%) are expressly exempted; (b) most school district special taxes are government-placed and already need 2/3 — Prop 43 doesn't change that; (c) fire measures like Sonoma Measure H were citizen-initiated, so genuinely affected. So the "No" case's strongest examples are: Sonoma Measure H (fire), Alameda Measure B (healthcare), LA Measure A (homelessness), Santa Clara Measure D (open space), Crockett parcel tax, SF Prop H (transit), RTM (transit).

Also note the Yes campaign's claim "2,000 new or higher local taxes in the past decade" — most of those required 2/3 anyway (government-placed), so the claim is inflated relative to what Prop 43 changes. And the claim about "6% real estate transfer taxes costing a $54,000 homeowner" — Prop 43's prospective effect on transfer taxes is limited (transfer taxes are special taxes? They're transactions taxes; if a charter city imposes a documentary transfer tax by initiative, then 2/3 would apply; the ad valorem prohibition in (b) may also matter). But the withdrawn initiative's transfer-tax cap is NOT in Prop 43 — the Yes campaign's argument text still emphasizes real estate transfer taxes ("Protects homeowners from costly new real estate taxes"), which somewhat overstates. Let me verify whether the argument in favor overstates by referencing transfer taxes.

The Pro argument says: "Prop. 43 protects homeowners from costly new real estate taxes... Some cities now charge real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%." Under Prop 43, could a city still impose a new real estate transfer tax? If imposed by initiative as a special tax → 2/3 needed. If imposed by a city council → already 2/3 needed (as a special tax) or if it's a general tax, majority. Also, subdivision (b) bars ad valorem taxes on real property via initiative. Transfer taxes are arguably "transactions taxes" — Art XIII D Sec 3(a) prohibits local governments from imposing "ad valorem taxes on real property, or transactions or rights or privileges on property" except the 1% cap and bond repayment. Courts (e.g., Building Industry Assn. v. City of San Jose? or the 2025 Measure ULA litigation) — in LA's case, the superior court in 2025? Let me check quickly: "Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn v. City of Los Angeles" — In June 2025, a Los Angeles Superior Court judge ruled Measure ULA invalid? Hmm. Actually I recall in 2025 the California Court of Appeal upheld ULA (Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn. v. City of Los Angeles (2025) 108 Cal.App.5th ...?) holding ULA is not an "ad valorem tax" barred by Article XIII D. Let me verify with a quick search, since Prop 43's section (b) interacts with this.

Anyway, that's a detail. Let me check the LA Times endorsement and the Measure ULA case status for completeness, then decide.

Actually — one more important consideration: Prop 43's section (b) says no local government (including via initiative) may impose ad valorem taxes on real property except as provided in Art XIII D Sec 3(a)(2) (bond taxes). Note it omits the Art XIII D Sec 3(a)(1) exception? It says "except as provided in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D" — per the text I fetched: "(b) ... may impose ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D." Yes, paragraph (1) = the 1% cap exception. Fine — that essentially codifies existing law but extends it to the initiative power. Note that this could bar things like "split roll" style local measures or mansion-tax-like ad valorem taxes. LA's Measure ULA is a transfer tax on sales price value — could be characterized as ad valorem on the transaction. If courts treat Prop 43(b) as extending the Art XIII D ban on "ad valorem taxes on real property" to initiatives, then future ULA-style measures via initiative are barred outright (not just 2/3). That's a substantive change beyond the vote threshold — and the LAO/Attorney General summary does not mention subdivision (b) at all! Interesting: The official title and summary mentions only the two-thirds threshold, and the LAO analysis doesn't mention the ad valorem prohibition. The Hoover analysis flags it as a "second provision that has drawn less attention."

That's a notable transparency problem: a constitutional provision with potentially large effects (barring voter-initiated ad valorem property taxes, e.g., mansion taxes, split-roll style local taxes) that the LAO didn't analyze. Hmm, though arguably it just restates existing law (Art XIII A Sec 1(a) 1% cap and Art XIII D Sec 3), so the practical change is limited to the initiative power.

Let me quickly check the ULA litigation status to see whether courts already bar charter-city transfer taxes, which would make (b) less consequential.

Then finalize with a "no" recommendation, but let me steelman "yes" once more.

Steelman yes:
- The Upland loophole has been exploited at industrial scale: "hundreds of special tax increases — mostly sales taxes — have been enacted with simple majority votes" (per Daniel Borenstein's CalMatters commentary, Aug 2026). Hmm, that's a claim from an anti-43? No — Borenstein is typically a fiscal hawk; the quote says "Since then, hundreds of special tax increases — mostly sales taxes — have been enacted with simple majority votes, and dozens more are pending because, if passed, Prop. 43 would reinstate the two-thirds vote requirement." Wait, that quote suggests a rush to pass taxes before Jan 1, 2027. If hundreds of special taxes have passed by simple majority, the fiscal impact is large, and the "loophole" is being used massively — which strengthens the Yes case (and the "rush" behavior suggests governments are gaming).

Hmm, "hundreds" vs. CalMatters' "two dozen" — the two dozen refers to measures passing with less than 2/3. Many citizen-initiated special taxes pass with more than 2/3 anyway. Let me check that claim: CalMatters says "Since then cities and counties have passed two dozen of these measures by margins of less than two-thirds."

But wait — Borenstein's "hundreds of special tax increases — mostly sales taxes — have been enacted with simple majority votes" might be inaccurate/exaggerated. Let me read that commentary to check. It's "Five ballot items ask: 'Who should pay billions in taxes?'" — Aug 2026.

Let me also check the "rush to the ballot" phenomenon: how many citizen-initiated special taxes are on Nov 2026 local ballots (dozens pending). That's evidence of gaming/timing arbitrage, supporting Yes. But it's also evidence that these are wanted by communities.

I'll check that article quickly. Also LA Times endorsement.

Let me weigh the final decision. I'm leaning "no" based on:
- Restricting the initiative power and majority rule.
- Documented harms to fire, health, transit, homelessness funding at a time of federal cuts.
- Concentrated funding from commercial real estate/business interests who are the tax payers.
- Distortionary effects (shift to fees/sales taxes/general taxes, less transparency).
- Narrow benefit (only affects citizen-initiated special taxes; most local special taxes already require 2/3 and most pass).

But let me consider the counterargument that special taxes are bad policy in general (earmarking reduces flexibility), and that requiring broad consensus for permanent earmarked taxes is good governance. Also the "no sunset, permanent half-cent sales tax passed with 55.7%" example is genuinely troubling.

Hmm. There's a real tension. Let me think about which error is worse.

If Yes passes: local special taxes via initiative need 2/3. Effect: fewer new earmarked local taxes; local governments shift to general taxes (majority), fees, bonds; some services underfunded; minority veto power. Over 10 years, maybe $X billion less local revenue. Given that most special taxes are government-placed and already require 2/3 and still pass ~60-75% of the time, the marginal effect is on the subset of measures that would win 50-66% — roughly 30% of transportation LOSTs historically, and the ~two dozen high-profile ones since 2017.

If No passes (status quo): continued erosion of the 2/3 rule for special taxes; more special taxes enacted with slim margins; increased earmarking of local revenues; more "initiative laundering" by governments. Also continued uncertainty and litigation.

From a "what makes California better governed" standpoint: I think the more compelling consideration is that California's local governments are already among the most fiscally constrained in the nation, and this constraint has produced documented harms (underfunded services, regressive revenue mixes, housing crisis contributions). Adding another supermajority barrier to one of the few remaining revenue paths — while the measure's funding comes overwhelmingly from commercial real estate interests seeking to block business/property taxes — is net harmful for the median Californian. Moreover, the measure's own author opposes it, and it was drafted under duress.

Additionally, the ad valorem provision (b) is a sleeper with unclear reach that the LAO didn't analyze.

I'll go with "no."

But let me do a few more checks to make sure I'm not missing something that would flip this: e.g., evidence that citizen-initiated special taxes are disproportionately self-serving (proponents get the money) — HJTA's claim. Let me check a couple of examples: SF Prop C (2018) was funded by Marc Benioff and directed to homelessness services (not to the sponsor). LA Measure ULA — sponsored by Unite Here/CEDA, revenue to affordable housing (not to sponsor, though unions benefit from construction jobs). Alameda Measure B (healthcare) — sponsored by healthcare unions? Measure W? Sonoma Measure H — sponsored by firefighters union/local government (firefighters benefit). Fresno transportation sales tax initiative — sponsored by developers/business? The Bay Area RTM — created by SB 63 with transit agencies; revenue goes to transit agencies (sponsors are labor/transit advocates). LA County Measure A — sponsored by labor/nonprofits.

So in several cases, the sponsors are entities that benefit from the spending (unions, transit agencies, healthcare providers). HJTA's "direct all the money to themselves" claim has some force: e.g., firefighter-sponsored fire taxes, SEIU-sponsored healthcare taxes, construction-labor-sponsored transit taxes. This is the classic "tax-and-spend coalition" problem: interest groups that receive the revenue can pass taxes on the general public with a slim majority. That's a genuine concern about the initiative-tax path — arguably a bigger concern than the "minority veto" issue, since it involves concentrated beneficiaries imposing diffuse costs.

Hmm, that's a strong argument for Yes actually. In public choice terms: requiring a 2/3 supermajority for taxes that earmark revenue to specific groups forces broader consensus and prevents narrow coalitions (unions + providers) from taxing the general public for their own benefit with 51%.

But the counter: many of these taxes fund broadly valued public goods (fire protection, healthcare for the poor, transit) that under-funded local governments can't otherwise provide; and the 2/3 rule empowers a well-funded minority (business groups) to block. Both are "special interests."

Which framework should dominate? Let's consider outcomes: California's local services are visibly underfunded (transit on the brink of cuts, homelessness crisis, wildfire). Would requiring 2/3 improve outcomes? It would reduce revenue for earmarked services; but the "No" side notes that Prop 13's constraints led to fee/sales-tax reliance. On the other hand, earmarked taxes reduce budgetary flexibility, which many fiscal experts criticize (LAO has long criticized special taxes/earmarks).

Hmm. Honestly this is close. Let me look for more evidence: the Tax Policy Center article ("California's Proposition 43 Adds a New Chapter to State's History of Local Tax Limits") may have a balanced assessment. And maybe an academic take. Also let's check the Mercury News / SF Chronicle YES reasoning, and the LA Times (probably NO). Also check "Californians for Fiscal Responsibility" or any notable No-on-43 arguments about school funding being exempt.

California’s Proposition 43 Adds a New Chapter to State’s History of Local Tax Limits
Aravind Boddupalli
Display Date
October 27, 2026
Next month, California voters will decide whether to require a two-thirds vote for voter-initiated local special taxes, or taxes dedicated to a specific purpose.
Proposition 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) would reverse a series of court decisions (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2021/a157983.html) that have allowed these measures to pass with a simple majority, raising their approval threshold to the same one that local lawmakers face to enact these taxes. If passed, it would apply to measures placed on ballots on or after January 1, 2027.
While cities, counties, and special districts provide essential services, including fire protection, roads, parks, and libraries, their ability to raise taxes is governed by a complicated set of statewide rules. Proposition 43 could further constrain local governments’ ability to raise revenue, even for services supported by a majority of voters.
California’s fiscal history and comparisons with other states offer some perspective on what the change could mean for local governments and the communities they serve.
California's fiscal rules are nearly 50 years in the making
Proposition 43 joins a lineage of statewide measures (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Detail/2669) that reshaped local public finances starting in the late 1970s. A few notable examples:
Proposition 13 (1978) capped property tax rates and required two-thirds voter approval for local special taxes, which later came to be defined as taxes dedicated to special purposes.
Proposition 218 (1996) added restrictions on local governments' ability to raise revenue, including new simple majority voter-approval requirements for new general taxes and property-related fees.
Proposition 39 (2000) lowered the voter threshold for qualifying school facility bonds from two-thirds to 55 percent, moving in the opposite direction.
Proposition 26 (2010) broadened the definition of taxes subject to voter approval.
The result is a complicated set of institutional rules where revenue changes face different voter-approval requirements depending on their type, how revenue will be used, and whether voters or legislators placed the proposal on the ballot.
California is not the only state revisiting supermajority requirements in November. Voters in South Dakota and Utah (https://www.multistate.us/elections/ballot-measure?id=21126) will consider measures that would require higher approval thresholds for certain tax or constitutional changes. But California's debate is different: It centers on voter-initiated local tax measures rather than statewide tax initiatives or statewide constitutional amendments.
The California Budget and Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/) identifies several recent voter-initiated special taxes that passed with a simple majority vote. Examples include San Francisco’s tax on commercial landlords to raise funds for child care and early education, and Fresno’s increase of its local sales tax rate to fund community parks.
What the revenue patterns reveal
According to TPC’s analysis of the 2024 Census Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances (https://state-local-finance-data.taxpolicycenter.org/pages.cfm), California ranked 37 th among states on the share of local general revenue coming from own-source revenues, like taxes, fees, or charges, rather than federal or state government transfers (Figure 1).
Since 1977, just before Proposition 13 began reshaping California's local finances, growth in local own-source revenue has trailed growth in state own-source revenue, although some of this reflects different tax bases at each government level, including the state's reliance on income taxes and local governments' heavier reliance on property taxes and fees (Figure 2).
Together, these figures suggest that California's local governments remain somewhat reliant on state decisions and intergovernmental funding streams. However, local governments continue to deliver many public services. This disconnect can weaken efficiency and accountability, as noted (https://lao.ca.gov/analysis_1993/MGMS_reprint_02-93.html) by the state's Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO).
And, if Proposition 43 makes it more challenging for local governments to raise revenues, local lawmakers may need to increase general taxes, reduce government spending, or look to state lawmakers to help foot their bills. Unlike special taxes, general taxes are not earmarked to be spent for a particular purpose. Voters who support a tax that specifically pays for child care or community parks may be less willing to support a general tax that goes into a government's general fund and could be spent across a wide range of activities.
Further, localities within California differ substantially in wealth, economic opportunity, and fiscal capacity. Jurisdictions with stronger property tax bases and local economies can often generate more revenue from the same available tax policy than communities with fewer resources (https://www.gfoa.org/materials/addressing-resource-inequities). If dedicated local revenues from special taxes are harder to secure, those disparities in fiscal capacity and maintenance of services between poorer and wealthy jurisdictions could widen, raising potential equity (https://taxpolicycenter.org/publications/state-and-local-government-revenues-and-racial-disparities) concerns (https://taxpolicycenter.org/publications/more-than-fines-and-fees-incorporating-equity-city-revenue-strategies).
California has seen before how voting rules affect tax measures
Prior research (https://www.ppic.org/publication/fiscal-effects-of-voter-approval-requirements-on-local-governments/) found that voter approval rates vary considerably by type of revenue measure, with transportation, fire protection, and education-related measures receiving the most support.
And after Proposition 39 lowered the approval threshold for school facility bond measures in 2000, passage rates increased by nearly 30 percent, according to the LAO (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Detail/2978), even though average share of voters supporting the measures remained roughly flat.
California’s voting rules create a contradiction
Voters often prefer taxes dedicated to a specific purpose (https://www.californiacityfinance.com/ReformVoteSwap.pdf), yet California generally requires higher approval thresholds for those taxes than for general taxes.
Proposition 43 would extend the two-thirds approval requirement, which currently applies to local lawmakers, to voters who propose local special taxes. Supporters could argue that requiring broader agreement protects taxpayers from increases that lack widespread support. But the higher threshold would also make it harder to pass tax measures that a majority of voters do support.
California’s history suggests that voter-approval thresholds matter. The question facing voters in November is whether requiring broader support for local special taxes is worth potentially limiting communities’ ability to raise revenue for public services.

Schaben, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images In summary The measure would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes, instead of the simple majority for citizen-led initiatives. Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure? Issue Brief
Should California Voters Approve Proposition 43?
What the Supermajority Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives Would Mean for California Communities
August 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would require that at least two-thirds of local voters approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax, starting on January 1, 2027. As communities across California are facing substantial challenges and uncertainties, this measure would make it harder for local voters to raise revenues to support local public services and give outsized power to a small share of voters. Approval of the measure would decrease the likelihood that local governments meet the needs of their residents and could increase hardship in some communities throughout the state.
